title: The Southward Offensive
subtitle: A Desna crossing threatens the rear of the Soviet armies in Ukraine
author: Robert M. Dobo
phase: III — The Battle for Strategic Objectives
summary: A bridge at Novgorod-Seversky opened the way behind the Soviet Dnieper defence. The response exposed the difficulty of moving armies, supplies and civilian labour while German occupation violence escalated farther west.
body:
A crossing changes the problem

On 26 August 1941, the 3rd Panzer Division gained a usable bridge across the Desna at Novgorod-Seversky (now Novhorod-Siverskyi). Beyond it lay the communications of the Soviet armies defending Ukraine. Those armies still faced principally westward along the Dnieper; Guderian’s troops could now advance south behind them. The bridge mattered because tanks, infantry and supply columns could cross it together, turning a local penetration into a threat to an entire front. Soviet headquarters acknowledged the loss of the town in its report the following morning. Its order of 29 August identified the breach on the left of the 13th Army and sought to strike back. The Germans had opened a route. The Soviet command still had an opportunity to close it. [1] The crossing was an early result of the turn examined in The Decision to Turn South. No fresh German army had appeared in Ukraine. Heinz Guderian’s 2nd Panzer Group and Maximilian von Weichs’s 2nd Army were moving from Army Group Centre’s southern wing while other formations took over their positions. Farther south, Gerd von Rundstedt’s Army Group South still contested the Dnieper. Cooperation between these forces depended on separate battles succeeding in sequence. On 26 August, Kiev remained outside any completed encirclement, and the southern pincer had yet to make its decisive northward advance. [2] The starting problem was the survival of substantial Soviet forces after two months of retreat. David Stahel’s study of Kiev emphasises that the German victory later associated with this campaign emerged from an army already experiencing serious attrition. Army Group South had failed to dispose of the Southwestern Front through its own opening operations, while its motorised formations had accumulated losses and mechanical wear. Assistance from the north offered a way around resistance that frontal pressure had not removed. This interpretation gives the campaign a more demanding explanation than the familiar image of an effortless armoured sweep: German operational opportunity and German material weakness developed together. The southward offensive attempted to exploit the former before the latter made another major undertaking impossible. [3] For Soviet commanders, the threat was more complicated than an approaching column. The Germans were moving near the junction between two fronts, the large Soviet commands responsible for several armies. Holding a river line depended on neighbouring formations remaining in contact, reporting promptly and sharing a workable understanding of the enemy’s direction. The fighting now tested all three conditions. It also exposed a difficult choice: divisions moved north to protect the flank would be unavailable along the Dnieper, where the Germans were preparing crossings of their own. The Soviet response was therefore an attempt to preserve an entire connected defensive system while its northern attachment was coming under attack. [4]

The offensive’s unequal moving parts

Guderian’s account places the opening movement on 25 August. XXIV Motorised Corps sent the 3rd Panzer Division towards Novgorod-Seversky, with the 10th Motorised Division moving through Kholmy and Avdeyevka. The 4th Panzer Division first had to finish fighting near the Sudost before following. XLVII Motorised Corps protected the eastern flank. By the evening of 26 August, the 3rd Panzer Division was at the Desna crossing, whereas the 4th remained engaged southeast of Starodub and the 17th Panzer Division fought near Semtsy, south of Pochep. These dispositions describe an offensive assembling through combat, rather than a compact formation already moving at a single speed. [5] Guderian’s leading tanks represented only part of his command. A panzer group combined armoured and motorised formations with artillery, engineers and supporting services; the whole organisation had to sustain the penetration. The American Army’s operational history describes substantial strength left to contain Bryansk Front. Those formations protected the advance but could not simultaneously reinforce its spearhead. Soviet resistance beside the German route therefore mattered even when it failed to stop the leading division. It obliged Guderian to divide the force with which he hoped to turn the Soviet position. [2] Infantry armies performed a related but different task. Weichs’s 2nd Army approached the northern side of the Ukrainian theatre after the fighting around Gomel. Its progress brought pressure against Soviet formations that might otherwise have turned against Guderian’s western flank. Yet infantry could not simply reproduce the movement of selected motorised detachments. It had its own defended routes to open, artillery to bring forward and marching columns to supply. A successful armoured advance could thus increase the distance between the spearhead and the infantry expected to make its gains secure. The operational relationship was reciprocal: the tanks created a threat deep in the Soviet rear, while the infantry helped prevent that threat from becoming an isolated excursion. [2] There was a further complication in the organisation of Soviet command. A Bryansk Front order issued at 18.00 on 25 August transferred the forces of the Central Front to Bryansk Front from midnight at the beginning of 26 August. It then prescribed a new army composition, with some arrangements taking effect on 28 August. Andrei Yeremenko’s headquarters was consequently absorbing formations and establishing control while the Germans were attacking the same geographical seam. This was more than the replacement of one name on a map. Existing reports, supply relationships and subordinate headquarters had to be fitted into a new command structure during a moving battle. [1] The evening report for 26 August shows how unevenly that process worked. Communications with 50th Army functioned by telephone, telegraph and liaison officers; the telegraph and radio connections with 13th Army were intermittent. An operational group was being established around Khutor-Mikhailovsky to control forces inherited from Central Front. These details help explain why a headquarters could possess a strategic appreciation of danger without possessing an accurate, timely picture of every threatened crossing. Recognising the danger was only the beginning of a response. A report had to reach headquarters, produce an order suited to the forces available, and return through the damaged communications network before the threatened formation’s position changed again. [1]

Rivers, roads and the new Soviet flank

The Desna, Seym and Dnieper formed connected obstacles rather than three interchangeable blue lines. The Desna approached the Dnieper from the northeast, while the Seym fed into the Desna farther upstream. A German advance from the Starodub region towards the rear of the Southwestern Front therefore encountered successive river valleys and a limited set of useful crossings. Securing one passage did not provide an uninterrupted road to Kiev’s eastern communications. It changed the next military problem: Soviet forces could contest the bridgehead, threaten its approaches or hold another river farther south. The Southwestern Front’s orders consequently identified routes towards Krolevets, Vorozhba and Konotop, as well as stretches of riverbank. The command was trying to protect a network through which the enemy could penetrate. [4] The creation of the 40th Army gave this concern an institutional form. Assigned to the Southwestern Front on 26 August under Kuzma Podlas, the army was placed on its endangered northern side. The detailed directive issued two days later listed the 293rd and 135th Rifle Divisions, the 10th Tank Division, the 2nd Airborne Corps and the 5th Antitank Artillery Brigade among its formations. Its headquarters was to be at Konotop. The task was to prevent a breakthrough towards the routes just identified and protect the front against attack from the north. These were concrete defensive responsibilities, even though the order’s list of formations cannot by itself establish their actual strength, equipment or readiness at every moment. [4] The presence of airborne troops is instructive. In this setting an airborne corps designation did not imply that the formation was about to conduct a parachute operation. The directive required elements of the 2nd Airborne Corps to be brought by motor transport to the Korop–Maloye Ustye sector. It also ordered the 3rd Airborne Corps to concentrate by road in the Konotop area by the morning of 31 August. Their usefulness rested on the availability of organised infantry that could be shifted towards a threatened point. Their mobility rested on trucks, suitable roads and time. An airborne title did not exempt soldiers from the transport constraints affecting the rest of the army. [4] The same directive required the 5th Army to continue holding the Dnieper while protecting itself against attack from the north. At least one division was to defend a specified stretch of the Desna by the end of 29 August; at least two divisions were to be retained near the junction with 40th Army. The 37th Army had to hold Kiev, with its flanks tied to the Dnieper and its centre occupying the fortified approaches west of the city. The 26th and 38th Armies continued the defence farther south. Each instruction was intelligible in isolation. Together they reveal the strain of trying to preserve a long river front while constructing a second front at an angle to it. [4] Nor was every formation immediately available for the task assigned to it. The document placed the 304th Rifle Division in reserve while it completed its armament and left the 81st Rifle Division reorganising around Lubny. Such details correct the impression created by orderly symbols on a situation map. A division could exist in an order of battle while still requiring weapons, replacement personnel or reorganisation before effective employment. The northern defence was therefore a race between the German advance and the Soviet ability to turn administrative assignments into coordinated fighting power. That race remained open at the end of August; its outcome should not be read backward from the catastrophe of September. [4]

Resistance that consumed the advance

The Bryansk Front reports show local resistance continuing beside the German breakthrough. At Semtsy, south of Pochep, the Germans attacked after repeated air bombardment and took the settlement during the afternoon of 26 August. The following morning’s Soviet report stated that a counterattack had recovered it at 22.00. These are headquarters reports, not a complete reconstruction of the engagement, but their sequence is revealing. On the same day that the Germans gained a major crossing farther south, a nearby sector was changing hands through attack and counterattack. The front was not dissolving uniformly. Its unevenness forced German commanders to decide where to press ahead and where to employ troops that might otherwise have joined the main thrust. [1] By 29 August, Yeremenko had ordered a mobile group under Arkady Yermakov to attack towards the threatened sector. The grouping combined the 108th Tank Division, 141st Tank Brigade and 4th Cavalry Division. The order prescribed separate routes, Sudost crossings and successive objectives, with the intended arrival around Novgorod-Seversky by the end of 31 August. The cavalry was to follow behind the tank formations and cooperate in destroying the opposing forces. This was an effort to strike the side of the penetration and restore the connection between Soviet armies. Its existence establishes a deliberate response; the ambitious deadlines establish the command’s expectations, not proof that the objectives were reached. [1] The arrangements for cooperation are as revealing as the movement arrows. The air command was instructed to cover the mobile group’s march and crossings, support its attacks, and send an operational officer and a U-2 aircraft to each of the principal armoured formations. A radio centre was to be established around Trubchevsk. These provisions addressed practical weaknesses that earlier fighting had exposed: formations needed to find one another, communicate their positions and connect air attacks with ground movement. The order does not demonstrate that these arrangements worked smoothly. It does demonstrate that Soviet command was attempting to solve a coordination problem, rather than merely supplying another mass of troops to an undifferentiated counterattack. [1]

A minefield on the wrong side of the report

The Bryansk Front’s report for 26 August recorded a small incident involving the 108th Tank Division. Three T-40 light tanks conducting reconnaissance near Sloboda entered a minefield laid by Soviet troops. A lieutenant was killed, a Red Army soldier wounded and two tanks put out of action. The report gives no names and does not establish who failed to pass on the minefield’s location. It nevertheless preserves a human and mechanical cost that disappears in a map showing only German and Soviet positions. Defensive preparations could become a danger to friendly movement when information failed to travel with them. The division was in front reserve, preparing for employment against the German penetration; its losses here occurred before such a contest could be reduced to a comparison of opposing tank strengths. This is a documented accident, not evidence that all Soviet minefields or reconnaissance procedures were equally defective. [1]

Moving supplies and making roads

Bryansk Front’s rear-services directive of 25 August provides an unusually clear view of what sustaining the response required. Its armies were assigned railway sections leading through Bryansk and the approaches from Orel and Dmitriyev-Lgovsky. Ammunition stocks were to be built at several levels: with the troops, at army depots and at front bases. Food and fodder reserves were likewise distributed, with fifteen days prescribed at front bases and smaller reserves farther forward. These were targets for an operating supply system. They must not be mistaken for evidence that every specified stock already existed. The order shows what headquarters wanted available as it prepared to defend, regroup and counterattack. [1] Every army was also to have at least two prepared roads suitable for motor and horse transport. Roads and bridges were to remain passable in different weather conditions, and local road authorities and the civilian population were to be used extensively to bring them into condition. Difficult stretches required traffic regulation and tractors ready to assist vehicles. The plan was due on the evening of 26 August, with the road preparations to be completed by 1 September. These deadlines placed repair work inside the battle’s timetable. A formation moving towards the Desna could be delayed by a damaged bridge or an obstructed approach even when its headquarters had fuel somewhere in the rear. [1] The directive placed civilian labour inside the supply plan. Local road authorities and inhabitants were to help make the routes usable, alongside military arrangements for traffic control and vehicle recovery. It does not establish how particular villages recruited workers, whether they volunteered or were compelled, or what protection their households received. The documented demand is nevertheless substantial: headquarters required civilian work on a fixed military deadline while the front was moving. This was one way the army’s effort to recover imposed duties on people behind it. The record counts the roads to be prepared; it leaves the workers’ individual circumstances largely unrecorded. [1] Medical evacuation ran in the opposite direction. The directive provided for wounded and sick personnel to move by hospital trains from Bryansk and Dmitriyev-Lgovsky towards the evacuation system around Orel, Livny, Yelets and Mtsensk. It also required army medical facilities to be organised near the principal rail connections. This was a planned chain of movement from fighting units to transport and onward treatment. Its dependence on rail access explains another consequence of the German penetration: a threatened communications route endangered both the arrival of ammunition and the removal of casualties. Holding a junction could preserve the possibility of care as well as the capacity to continue fighting. [1] German mobility depended on a similarly layered system, although one increasingly stretched away from its original bases. Fuel delivered to the theatre still had to reach the divisions; replacement parts still had to reach repair personnel; damaged vehicles still had to be recovered. The German Army’s early September assessment, summarised in its postwar American study, reported exhausted fuel stockpiles and shortages that sometimes interrupted operations in the south. Its 4 September tank assessment distinguished vehicles available for employment from those under repair and those disabled. Those later figures cannot describe every division on 26 August, but they confirm that the turn south was being executed during an accumulating maintenance problem, before autumn weather could provide an all-purpose explanation for German difficulties. [6]

Grossman’s road out of the retreat

Vasily Grossman’s notebooks from the retreat through Belarus and northeastern Ukraine preserve people whom operational reports usually leave unnamed. In the edited diary selection, an older woman waits beside a passing column in the hope of seeing her son. Others offer soldiers milk, cucumbers, apples and curds. Grossman also notices households being abandoned and refugees sharing roads with livestock, guns and military vehicles. These observations belong to the August–September journey; the published extract does not justify assigning each scene to 26 August. Their value lies in showing civilian action amid disruption. The people beside the road were searching, feeding, deciding what to carry and trying to maintain contact with relatives. Grossman was an involved Soviet correspondent, not a detached surveyor of public opinion, and his impressions cannot speak for every village. They nevertheless restore individual purposes to a landscape that military records chiefly describe as routes and obstacles. [7]

The southern front and the wider war

Farther south, Kleist’s 1st Panzer Group was still involved in the struggle for the Dnieper approaches. Southern Front’s report covering 15–31 August described combat around Dnepropetrovsk, Zaporozhye, Berislav and Kherson, alongside the regrouping and replenishment of Soviet formations. Its account dated the evacuation of Dnepropetrovsk to the early hours of 25 August, after sustained fighting on the approaches. These operations had their own objectives: crossings towards the industrial districts farther east, and approaches towards the Crimea in the lower river sector. They were not yet the northward movement from Kremenchuk that would later form the southern arm of the Kiev encirclement. [8] The lower river remained actively contested. A Soviet attempt to regain Kherson on 24 August failed; the same summary described renewed German pressure at Berislav on 26 August and the Soviet withdrawal across the river during the following night. On 30 August German troops established a foothold around Kakhovka after artillery and air preparation. These developments show why it is misleading to imagine Army Group South waiting in readiness for Guderian. Its formations were fighting their way through a broad river system against opponents still capable of resistance and counterattack. The later concentration for the decisive encirclement would require selection among these competing tasks. [8] Western policy operated on another timescale. In the Roosevelt–Churchill message transmitted officially to Moscow on 18 August, the two leaders proposed a conference to determine longer-term Soviet requirements and the allocation of shared resources. They promised continuing shipments while acknowledging that British and American resources, although large, had competing demands. This correspondence matters because it records a developing commitment to Soviet survival without implying that promised equipment was already available to Podlas or Yeremenko. A shipment leaving a Western port and a weapon reaching a threatened division were separate events, connected by voyages, unloading, assembly and onward transport. The immediate defence of the Desna still depended on the forces and material that Soviet commanders could bring into the battle at hand. [9]

Children beyond the operational map

The danger created by German occupation was already visible behind Army Group South. In her study of military chaplains, Doris Bergen examines the August murder of Jewish children at Bila Tserkva and the later accounts of German clergymen who had attempted an intervention. She also restores testimony from Jews whose experiences complicate a story centred entirely on those Germans. Isaac Piatsetski, a Polish Jewish refugee interviewed in 1998, remembered seeing a train evacuating children before the occupation. Bergen treats his belief about its eventual destination more cautiously than his recollection of the departure itself. The distinction matters: an evacuation could be a real act of rescue without every subsequent stage being recoverable from one witness. The contrast between children transported away and children trapped under German authority establishes what was at stake when military routes remained open. It also connects the displacement begun in Poland in 1939 with the new emergency in Soviet Ukraine. [10]

Farther west, conquest was already exposing entire communities to organised murder. At Kamenets-Podolsk, now Kamianets-Podilskyi, German killing units and forces under Higher SS and Police Leader Friedrich Jeckeln murdered Jewish residents and Jews deported from Hungary. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum dates the massacre to 26–28 August and identifies 23,600 as Jeckeln’s reported total. That figure belongs to the whole action, not to 26 August alone. Hungarian authorities had expelled people classified as foreign Jews, including people unable to prove Hungarian citizenship; German authorities then held them in occupied territory. The victims included families, not simply the adult men whom earlier German killings had often targeted. Deportation and murder were connected decisions by identifiable authorities. This escalation occurred while German armies were still fighting for the crossings farther east, and before Kiev had fallen. [11]

The position reached

By the end of 26 August, the Germans had gained a significant crossing and Soviet headquarters faced an urgent threat to the northern connection of the Ukrainian defence. They had not yet converted that opportunity into a closed pocket. The Soviet orders of the following days show additional formations being assigned, river sectors being reinforced and a counterstroke being organised against the penetration. They also expose the limits of that response: incomplete concentrations, formations still reorganising, interrupted communications and a transport system required to support several urgent purposes at once. The Germans benefited from those weaknesses while encountering enough resistance to consume strength along their expanding flanks. [1][4] The crossing forced Soviet headquarters to defend two directions at once. Divisions needed along the Dnieper were also needed on the northern flank; trucks carrying them competed with supply and medical transport. The following days would test whether those movements could restore a connected defence before the Germans pushed farther south. In the north, a different evacuation crisis was already unfolding. The Baltic Withdrawal follows the ships leaving Tallinn, the units they carried and the passengers for whom survival did not necessarily mean arrival at a Soviet port.

sourceMethod: Numbered citations link to specific passages and return to their first use. Orders establish instructions; reports preserve their authors’ information and claims. Retrospective testimony and military accounts are identified. The command documents are published Soviet transcriptions; the bridge is checked against both Soviet reporting and Guderian’s retrospective account. Grossman and Bergen are consulted extracts. Kamenets-Podolsk’s total covers 26–28 August. English paraphrases of Russian, Ukrainian, Estonian and German texts are by Ostkrieg unless a published translation is identified. Reproduced archival references do not imply direct archival inspection. Later consequences are dated explicitly. The companion map and its precision notes are unchanged by this prose review.
